articles.title: 2 killed, dozens hurt as gunfire erupts at homecoming block party in south Georgia
articles.summary: (AP) — Law enforcement officials are still working to determine just what happened when a chaotic homecoming party spanning a four-block radius of a southern...
articles.body:
VIENNA, Ga. (AP) — Law enforcement officials are still working to determine just what happened when a chaotic homecoming party spanning a four-block radius of a southern Georgia town erupted in gunfire early Sunday, leaving two people dead and nearly three dozen others injured.

Dooly County Sheriff Craig Peavy identified the two people killed as 21-year-old Jaquevion Jackson of Cordele and 23-year-old Macaleb Jackson of Hawkinsville, Georgia. He did not say if the two were related.

Some of the three dozen injured had gunshot wounds, Georgia Bureau of Investigation Chris Hosey said Sunday evening, but he could not provide a number.

"We're still trying to work through that," Hosey said during a news conference Sunday evening.

No arrests had been reported hours later, and authorities gave no possible motive for the gunfire.

The injured ranged in age from 14 to 51, and they were taken to several regional hospitals, Peavy said. Some were in critical condition Sunday evening and others were stable, he said.

More than 1,000 people attended the party

More than 1,000 people had gathered at the site, and more than 50 shots were fired in at least two locations about a block apart in Vienna, Peavy told WMAZ-TV. Vienna is a small, rural community about 130 miles (about 210 kilometers) south of Atlanta.

Deputies were near the scene when the shooting began, Peavy said, and after they arrived more gunfire erupted about a block away.

"We don't know if it's coming at us or someone else," he said. "You just have to keep doing what you're doing and hope you don't get hit by gunfire."

The incident took place over homecoming weekend for Dooly County High School.

One woman recalled rapid-fire shots and people running

Ashley Gee, 30, who lives in nearby Turner County and came to Vienna for the party, described to the Atlanta Journal-Constitution a constant barrage of gunfire, imitating the sound of rapid-fire shots.

"Like a machine gun," she said. "One person ran, and everybody started running."

The AJC said the party drew in people from other surrounding counties in south Georgia following a local high school football team's victory at a homecoming game Friday night.

The shooting was not at a school-sponsored event, said Sherrod Willaford, superintendent of the Dooly County School System.

"We recognize that its impact may reach many of our students, families, and staff," he said in a statement. Schools will open Monday, he said, but additional safety measures have been put in place. He did not specify what they are.

Peavy said the festivities began Friday night, and that it had "gone well" with "respect from the community" that evening as deputies patrolled the event.

Sheriff says deputies were on hand as shots were still being fired

But the party Saturday night was a "different story," he said.

"We're still working through the investigation to see what went wrong. But at large parties with people from different places, not just your locals, sometimes problems come," he said.

"Our deputies were just about on the scene when it happened. They were at the end of each, most directions of where the block party was being held. But it was so many people. And it was just hard to figure out what was going on," he said.

Peavy said the shooting was "a learning experience," for his law enforcement team.

"There's just hardly no way to know how to operate when something like that happens on the scene," he said. He later continued, "We thought we'd been involved with a lot of stuff. But sometimes it surprises, and it was overwhelming."

Vienna is about a 50-mile (80-kilometer) drive south on the Interstate 75 corridor from the central Georgia city of Macon, where authorities say 12 teens were wounded by gunfire during a confrontation between people at a birthday party the previous weekend a city park.

Deputies in Vienna found two people dead at the scene and multiple others who had been shot, officials said. Police also did not specify how many of the injured had been shot. The victims were taken to several hospitals for treatment, the GBI said.

Dooly County Coroner Brett Walls said the two men were pronounced dead at the scene with fatal gunshot wounds. He said multiple other people were also shot, calling the scene "horrific."

Walls told the AJC that multiple people were struck by bullets and roughly a dozen others were hurt while trying to flee.

"This doesn't — it's not supposed to — happen in a small town like that. It's something you hear on the news in bigger cities," Walls told the newspaper, adding hospitals were flooded with the injured. "And even in bigger cities, you don't hear that kind of a number."

Investigators are seeking suspects and a motive

Authorities have not said whether any suspects are in custody or being sought. No motive has been given for the shooting.

Vienna Mayor Eddie Daniels said the shooting was about a block from his house and he "saw a lot of blue lights." Daniels said he hadn't spoken with law enforcement officials yet and had no details about what had happened.

Daniels said the city hadn't issued any kind of permit for the block party and he didn't know if it was a homecoming party.

Georgia Bureau of Investigation spokesperson Lydia Bullard declined to answer questions about the shooting, saying it was an ongoing investigation.

Bauer reported from Madison, Wisconsin. Associated Press reporters Rebecca Boone in Boise, Idaho, and Anthony Izaguirre in New York contributed to this report.

articles.title: Carmarthen Triathlete was 'very sick' after swimming in 'dirty' water
articles.summary: A new project is using small sampling devices on triathletes to help test the water quality in Wales.
articles.body:
A triathlete who travels the world to take part in races says making his dreams come true comes with serious risk after one event led to him being "very sick" in hospital.

Andrew Jones, from Carmarthen, takes part in various events, and has even earned a slot in the Ironman World Championship in Kona, Hawaii this month.

But the triathlete said swimming in "dirty" open-water made him very unwell ahead of the event after he contracted Campylobacter — an infection caused by bacteria.

Triathlon Cymru said its Safer Blue Spaces project, which is the first of its kind, was now using small sampling devices on triathletes to test the water and provide reliable data on water quality in Wales.

Jones said contracting Campylobacter from polluted water was "pretty nasty".

"It made me very sick unfortunately. In the house on a Sunday evening, I felt really unwell," he said.

"My temperature went up, my heart rate went up, I was shaking uncontrollably and unfortunately went straight to A&E."

He added: "I was in just over a week before one of the biggest races of my life. So very bad timing.

"I was a little annoyed, to be honest, because I think we go into the water with confidence, knowing everything is great and that's a great place to swim... it made me think about swimming in that particular area again."

Triathlon Cymru hopes its Safer Blue Spaces project, in partnership with Swim Wales, Bangor University and Imperial College London, will be able to help.

To collect data for the project, some of the competitors from Barry's SWYD Sprint Triathlon in August were pulled to the side and small devices — about the size of a fifty-pence piece — were attached to the backs of their wetsuits.

The national governing body for triathlon in Wales said they are new sampling devices and used as part of a pioneering project funded by the insurance group Admiral.

Normally, race organisers test the water to see if it is safe for swimming. However, there are limitations to that type of sampling.

Samples are usually collected at just one or two locations shortly before the race, which means it does not provide detailed data.

These sampling devices follow the swimmers' exact route while they are in the water, thereby providing accurate information.

"For us as an organisation, knowing what's in our water is really important because we're putting athletes in the water," said Amy Jenner, Triathlon Cymru's head of development.

"Across Wales, we have roughly around 60 events a year, so we want to know what's in our water.

"So having the fund available to us to do all of the research and the testing allows us to then go back to the athletes, back to the event organisers, to National Resource Wales, Public Health Wales and say what the picture is with our waters in Wales."

Simon Webb, who organises the Barry SWYD Sprint Triathlon, said it was important that athletes could swim "without the risk of potentially getting ill".

Once the competitors have finished the swim, they come to the transition area, take off their wetsuits, and continue with the race.

The technical team then come along and cut off the sampling devices, ready to send to Bangor University.

Kate Herridge, a PhD student working on the project, said the next step was to "concentrate these water samples" and "find if any pathogens have attached themselves to the samplers".

"We're able to take them off, concentrate them and then detect them and see what's present within them."

Triathlon Cymru hopes that ,in the future, it'll be able to share this data with environmental agencies and water companies in order to improve knowledge of what's in the water, and take steps to improve the quality of seas, lakes and rivers.

articles.title: Bengaluru techie drowns in quarry during Instagram-group trek; body found after 2-day search
articles.summary: Bengaluru: 30-year-old UX designer Ganesh Anjaneya Vinay drowned in a water-filled quarry near Jigani on Oct 2; body found after a 2-day SDRF/NDRF search.
articles.body: BENGALURU: A holiday trek, organised through an Instagram group, ended in tragedy after a 30-year-old techie allegedly drowned in a water-filled stone quarry near Yellammanadoddi, close to Jigani, on Oct 2.His body was recovered Sunday morning, following a two-day search operation.The deceased, Ganesh Anjaneya Vinay, a resident of Halasuru, belonged to Vijayawada in Andhra Pradesh.According to the preliminary investigation, Vinay worked as an associate UX designer for a private firm in Bengaluru. Vinay, who had a master’s degree from IIT Delhi, was living in Bengaluru for the past four years.Vinay had joined a group of eight trekkers for the outing during the Gandhi Jayanti holiday weekend. Among those who joined the trek was Vinay’s fiancé, a veterinary doctor.During the outing, the group stopped at a huge stone quarry near Yellammanadoddi. Mining activity at the quarry had reportedly stopped around 15 years ago, and the abandoned pit had since filled with water. The group decided to swim in the quarry.According to police, the group members took a dive and were enjoying themselves when, at around 5.30pm, Vinay suddenly disappeared in the water.The other members tried to rescue him, but were unsuccessful. They alerted Jigani police, who rushed to the spot along with personnel from the fire and emergency services.Police and rescue teams searched the quarry and subsequently summoned personnel from State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) and National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), besides involving local divers in the operation.Jigani police later contacted Eshwar Malpe, a scuba diver known for undertaking underwater rescue operations, and his team from Malpe for assistance. After nearly two days of continuous efforts, rescuers finally located Vinay’s body around 9am Sunday.Based on a complaint filed by Vinay’s brother, Jigani police registered an unnatural death report (UDR).The trekking group had connected with each other through Instagram and had planned the trek through the social media group, a senior officer said. The Instagram account regularly shares details about trekking destinations on the outskirts of Bengaluru and in neighbouring districts.According to the members, they had been swimming for around one-and-a-half hours before Vinay drowned.What was meant to be a holiday trek and an adventurous outing ended in tragedy, leaving the group and Vinay’s family traumatised.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bengaluru | Silver Rate in Bengaluru | Bank Holidays in Bengaluru | Public Holidays in Bengaluru | Bengaluru AQI | Weather in Bengaluru | Petrol Price in Bengaluru | Diesel Price in Bengaluru | CNG Price in Bengaluru | LPG Price in BengaluruStay updated with the latest Bengaluru news. articles.title: The job interview question you don't have to answer
articles.summary: Experts explain what you should do if you are asked for your current salary during a job interview.
articles.body:
Prepare all you like, but there is often still one job interview question that leaves you feeling uncomfortable.

While employers in the UK are within their rights to ask you how much you get paid in your current role, applicants are not obliged to tell them.

Recruiters have been encouraged to stop posing questions about salary history and, in the EU, new rules will prevent them doing so.

But in the UK, there is still a chance of it coming up, so how best should you answer?

When interviewing or deciding on new staff, employers must not discriminate against an applicant based on so-called protected characteristics, including age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation.

Sometimes it feels like interviewers, and interviewees, tip-toe around the subject of money.

But Louise Rudd, a senior adviser at the workplace advice and conciliation service Acas, says there are no regulations that prevent employers from asking interviewees about their current salary, or their salary expectations.

She says employers, if they do want to know, should ask each applicant the same questions to ensure they are treated fairly.

A few years ago, a campaign was launched urging employers to stop asking new recruits how much they were paid in their previous jobs. It had its own hashtag - #EndSalaryHistory.

The Fawcett Society, which campaigns for women and gender equality, said that asking the question risked maintaining historic unfair differences in pay due to gender, race and disability inequality.

Rather than offering a salary based on skills, experience and performance, it meant employers rewarded an individual's perceived worth and negotiating skills instead, the society said.

The Recruitment and Employment Confederation supported the move, urging recruiters not to ask.

Employers in the EU will be banned from asking about salary history in new rules being rolled out across the bloc.

But that's not featured in Cabinet Office plans in the UK, which instead concentrates on telling employers to publish salary information in job adverts .

When you're going for a new job, you can reveal your current salary if you are happy to.

Some people asked by BBC News out and about in London suggested they would reply with an inflated salary - so they get paid more in the next job. However, the risks of lying in an interview can far outweigh the possible reward.

There are no requirements for you to disclose your salary if you don't want to.

Rudd says some people might prefer to give their salary expectations, or outline their understanding of the salary range for the role.

Recruitment firms often say applicants could instead focus on their skills and experience, so those are used as a measure of what they should be paid, not their salary history.

Shazia Ejaz, director of campaigns at the Recruitment and Employment Confederation, says jobseekers should approach questions about pay with "realism but also confidence".

"Candidates can focus on showcasing the value they bring, the benefits that matter most to them and to go to the interview knowing the market rate for the role," she says.

"Jobseekers who have done their homework on salaries and can explain the contribution they will make are in the strongest position to secure the right package."

articles.title: Russia may be using hidden 'lunchbox-size' drone devices to counter Ukraine defenses: expert
articles.summary: Russia may be hiding lunchbox-sized signal repeaters inside Kyiv to help guide deadly drones past defenses, a weapons expert told Fox News Digital.
articles.body: Russia may be concealing signal repeaters inside Ukrainian cities to help its long-range drones evade air defenses and strike with greater precision, a weapons expert told Fox News Digital. The Kyiv Post first reported the possible use of the small ground devices, or repeaters, which Draganfly CEO and co-founder Cameron Chell said form part of an expanding "mesh" network that allows Russian drones to relay encrypted signals across multiple connections, making drones and drone swarms far harder for Ukraine to disrupt and bring down through standard electronic jamming. Chell’s warning also came amid escalating diplomatic notices for the region, with Moscow urging foreign nationals and embassy staff to leave the capital Kyiv immediately on Oct. 3, highlighting "mortal danger" as Russian forces threatened further "massive retaliatory strikes." "Russia has come to the realization that innovation is going to have to win this war, to the point now where they are becoming the innovative leader in this war—not just in terms of tactics, strategy, and technology, but the entire mindset is shifting," Chell said. RUSSIA READIES NEW 500-MILE MISSILE AS WEAPON EXPERT WARNS OF 'TERMINAL END GAME SURPRISES' Mesh networks, Chell explained, allow drones and strategically placed ground-based repeaters to relay encrypted signals across multiple connections, making many Russian drone flights harder to disrupt. "The use of mesh networking is now making it increasingly hard for a defensive position to bring down Russian drones in an effective manner." "With real-time precision, Russia can also now take their drone device into a particular window," Chell warned. "You can take the device onto a particular portion of a bridge because you can make that real-time, last-minute decision live because you've got all these additional network connections that increase not just your bandwidth, but also your resilience in terms of being jammed," he added. RUSSIAN STRIKES CONTINUE FOLLOWING VISIT BY WITKOFF AND KUSHNER TO KYIV Moscow's rapid technological evolution on the battlefield comes alongside unusually precise strikes on critical infrastructure in Kyiv, including major river crossings. Ukrainian Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat confirmed Sept. 29 that Russian forces are integrating mesh networking into their drone fleet while upgrading onboard optics. "The enemy is using high-quality materials in its UAVs and increasing camera resolution, allowing the enemy to view the situation on the ground in detail and use these UAVs for various targets. And the use of mesh networks is indeed present. Of course, this is quite dangerous," Ihnat said, according to Ukrainska Pravda. "They are using the principles of mesh networking to combat the counter-drone measures taken by Ukraine to ensure that drones can't get through or that those Russian communication links are broken," Chell said. FBI WARNS BATTLEFIELD-STYLE DRONE ATTACKS COULD REACH US: 'ONLY A MATTER OF TIME' "If Russia had multiple nodes that could communicate with a device and could use the device to communicate with other devices swarming the area, Ukraine would be faced with multiple, maybe even hundreds of connections to have to break simultaneously in order to bring that drone down," he said. On Oct. 3, Serhii Beskrestnov, a defense technology adviser to the Ukrainian presidency, also warned that Russian forces may have hidden the small signal boosters, or these ground repeaters, inside Kyiv to extend drone control. "Such repeaters are difficult to find, but we must search for them. As long as they exist, shielding the city with electronic warfare will not be effective," Beskrestnov warned. Specifically, the repeaters are small concealed radio relay devices that receive and retransmit signals, extending the range of drone operators while helping maintain control in areas where direct communications or GPS signals may be disrupted. "The size of these repeaters is really about the size of a large lunchbox. They're very easy to conceal, and they don't have to be turned on all the time, so they're hard to detect electronically," Chell said. "Moving one or two or even three of these into a city the size of Kyiv can be hugely effective." RUSSIA EXPOSES NATO WEAPONS GAP AS TOP COMMANDER WARNS ‘THE MATH IS NOT IN FAVOR OF THE WEST’ Technical analysts also pointed to a Sept. 4 strike on the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) headquarters on Volodymyrska Street in central Kyiv as early evidence of the tactic. Tracking data reportedly showed no relay drones airborne during the strike, fueling concerns that hidden ground-based repeaters may have been used to maintain communications with the attacking drone. "They will be doing everything they can to move as many of these things not just into Kyiv, but at any location in the country, even operational battlefields," Chell said. "The reality is every time you put another node on a mesh network, you exponentially increase the efficiency, resiliency, and capability of that network." Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sept. 28 that while Ukraine intercepts about 70% of conventional Russian drones during mass attacks, interception rates fall to 57% against newer, faster jet-powered UAVs. UKRAINE’S BATTLEFIELD IS TRANSFORMING THE FUTURE OF NATO "It is obvious that the Russians are not preparing to stop the war – at least not at the moment," Zelenskyy said. "Next year Russia plans to spend US$12 billion just on producing jet-powered drones and loitering munitions. And that's only one category of weapons. Of course, this doesn't only relate to Ukraine," he added, according to Ukrainska Pravda. "Russia probably has the intention of, if needed, expanding this war," Chell warned, arguing that drones themselves are becoming secondary to the communications architecture that guides them. "The network is now the weapon, and the drone is what executes the desired result," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "This is an unbelievable moment in the tactics of what's unfolding here with the future of warfare," Chell concluded.

articles.body:
Flávio Bolsonaro e Lula — Foto: Evaristo Sá/AFP e Amanda Perobelli/Reuters

As duas cidades mais católica e evangélica do Rio Grande do Sul tiveram resultados semelhantes no primeiro turno das eleições de 2026.

Em Montauri , apontada como a cidade mais católica do Brasil, e em Arroio do Padre , considerada a mais evangélica do país, Flávio Bolsonaro conquistou ampla maioria dos votos.

Em Montauri, município com menos de 1,5 mil habitantes, Flávio Bolsonaro recebeu 935 votos, o equivalente a 75,89% do total . Já Lula somou 187 votos, ou 15,18%.

O cenário foi ainda mais favorável a Flávio Bolsonaro em Arroio do Padre, cidade com pouco mais de 2,5 mil moradores . No município, ele obteve 1.976 votos, correspondentes a 82,54% dos votos . Lula teve 257 votos, o que representa 10,74%.

Igrejas em Montauri e Arroio do Padre, respectivamente — Foto: Reprodução/ RBS TV

Em Montauri, a fé católica está esculpida nas fachadas das casas, nas mãos que limpam a igreja aos domingos e nas promessas cumpridas com devoção. Dados do Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística (IBGE), divulgados no dia 6 de junho de 2025, mostraram que 98,3% dos 1366 entrevistados são fiéis da Igreja Católica.

Montauri, assim como as outras oito cidades gaúchas que estão entre as dez mais católicas do país, tem colonização italiana .

Igreja Católica, em Montauri, no RS — Foto: Reprodução/ RBS TV

Já em Arroio do Padre, a tradição evangélica luterana pulsa nos cultos, nas torres das igrejas e nas histórias que atravessam gerações desde os primeiros imigrantes pomeranos.

Dos 2.599 habitantes de Arroio do Padre, na região Sul, quase 88,7% da população ouvida pelo Censo de 2022 disse seguir a religião evangélica . Proporção que cresceu nos últimos anos, visto que, no Censo realizado em 2010, 86% da população dizia ser evangélica. A pesquisa conversou com 2.353 pessoas com mais de 10 anos de idade no município.

A religião luterana, vertente evangélica, veio em 1850 com as primeiras famílias pomeranas que se instalaram na localidade onde hoje fica Arroio do Padre.

O município tem apenas duas comunidades católicas, São Luiz e Sagrada Família, segundo a Arquidiocese de Pelotas. Ambas ficam na região da colônia, no interior do município.

articles.summary: Com 27 deputados eleitos, o PL ampliou sua força e seguirá com a maior bancada da Alesp. O PT elegeu 16 parlamentares e manteve a segunda posição, enquanto PSOL e PSD conquistaram nove cadeiras cada.
articles.body:
Fachada da Assembleia Legislativa de São Paulo (Alesp) — Foto: Divulgação/Alesp

Os eleitores paulistas escolheram neste domingo (4) os 94 deputados estaduais que vão representar a população na Assembleia Legislativa de São Paulo (Alesp) pelos próximos quatro anos.

A disputa teve cerca de 23,2 milhões de votos válidos e 3 milhões de votos brancos e nulos. As abstenções bateram recorde: mais de 7,6 milhões de pessoas deixaram de comparecer às urnas, o equivalente a aproximadamente 22,5% dos 34,1 milhões de eleitores aptos a votar no estado.

O PL foi o principal vencedor da disputa para a Assembleia Legislativa, elegendo 27 deputados estaduais , quase um terço das cadeiras da Casa. A legenda foi impulsionada pela votação recorde de Eduarda Campopiano, que recebeu 1,95 milhão de votos e se tornou a candidata mais votada da eleição (veja lista completa abaixo) .

O resultado consolidou a força do campo político liderado pelo governador reeleito Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos) . Somadas ao PL, as bancadas do PSD, União Brasil, Podemos, PP, Republicanos e MDB elegeram 63 dos 94 deputados estaduais, garantindo ao Palácio dos Bandeirantes uma base confortável para aprovar projetos e conduzir a agenda do governo nos próximos quatro anos

Na oposição, o PT elegeu a segunda maior bancada da Alesp. Impulsionado pela expressiva votação de Eduardo Suplicy, segundo deputado estadual mais votado do estado, o partido elegeu 16 parlamentares, mas perdeu uma cadeira em relação à composição da legislatura que se encerra.

Já o PSOL consolidou-se como a terceira força da Assembleia e ampliou sua presença ao eleger nove deputados estaduais.

articles.title: Newspaper headlines: Badenoch's 'bonfire of green laws' and 'Drop in global dealmaking'
articles.summary: Monday's front pages include stories about Kemi Badenoch at the start of the Tory conference, plus reports on global finance , abuse in schools and a BBC romance.
articles.body:
The Daily Telegraph says Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has launched legal action against Thames Valley Police over his arrest earlier this year. The former Duke of York was detained on suspicion of misconduct in public office, after the release of the Epstein files. Mountbatten-Windsor has consistently denied any wrongdoing. The report says he has asked a judge to determine whether search warrants that allowed police to raid his homes were lawful. The paper notes it is the first legal challenge of its kind by a royal since King Charles I in 1649.

The New York Times is reporting that the US has withdrawn all of its B-1 Air Force bombers from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire because of new threats about an Iran-backed plot. Six men have been arrested and released on bail in connection with a suspected terror plot at the base last month. The Wall Street Journal claims a branch of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps recruited UK nationals to carry out an attack.

According to the Guardian, thousands of sexual offences by children against other children are reported to the police in England and Wales every year. It says on average almost five crimes a day against children aged 12 and younger are recorded in primary and secondary schools. The children's commissioner for England, Dame Rachel de Souza, describes peer-on-peer abuse in schools as "widespread" and "normalised", but says important steps have been taken to tackle it in recent years.

The Daily Mirror says the Conservatives' plan to cut benefits while scrapping the cap on earnings for free childcare shows they are the "same old Tories". "Bad to the future" reads the paper's headline. The Times leads on the pledge from party leader Kemi Badenoch to scrap environmental quangos, end Net Zero regulations and push through a third runway at Heathrow to end what she calls the "doom loop" of low economic growth. The Daily Mail calls it "Kemi's common sense blueprint".

Global dealmaking fell below $1tn in the third quarter of this year, for the first time since Donald Trump introduced his trade tariffs last year, according to the Financial Times . The paper says activity fell to $986bn, as high interest rates threaten to derail what it calls a "blockbuster period" for high-profile mergers and acquisitions.

articles.title: Four African leaders issue joint declaration as Ethiopia war escalates
articles.summary: Egyptian, Eritrean, Somali and Sudanese leaders also call for talks to end the civil war in Sudan.
articles.body:
Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan have called for political and peaceful solutions amid escalating conflicts across the region, including Sudan’s civil war and major fighting in Ethiopia.

The leaders of the four countries – Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki, Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud and Sudanese army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan – issued a joint declaration on Sunday following a meeting in New Alamein City in Egypt.

Ethiopia has accused Egypt, Eritrea and Sudan of backing the armed alliance fighting its government. Officials from all three countries have denied involvement.

Earlier on Sunday, el-Sisi said that cross-border challenges required “a dialogue, not confrontation”.

The joint declaration appeared to push back against several policies pursued by Ethiopia in recent years, highlighting widening rifts between Addis Ababa and its neighbours.

The declaration backed Sudan’s military-led government and called for a political process led by Sudanese parties.

Sudan has been at war since April 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). Sudan and Ethiopia have traded accusations of interference in Sudan’s civil war.

The declaration also said control of the Red Sea should remain with the coastal states, seemingly in response to landlocked Ethiopia’s pursuit of sovereign access to the sea and a naval presence.

Somalia’s Mohamud told Al Jazeera on Saturday that Mogadishu does not object to Ethiopia securing commercial access through Somali ports, provided it is agreed with Somalia.

Egypt and Sudan, which have long disputed Ethiopia’s Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Nile, warned against what they called “unilateral measures” that harm downstream states.

The joint declaration was issued as fighting escalated in Ethiopia between federal forces and a seven-group armed alliance, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which fought a brutal two-year war with the government that ended with a fragile peace deal in 2022.

Government and allied forces retook the city of Mekelle on Sunday after the TPLF said it “temporarily moved out of” Tigray’s regional capital to “operate from somewhere else”.

According to Ethiopian state media reports, former Tigray interim leader Abraham Belay said on Sunday that the federal government is preparing a new temporary administration for the region and hopes to hold regional elections within months.

Ethiopian officials have accused neighbouring Eritrea of directly backing the rebel alliance in Ethiopia’s civil war.

Eritrea’s Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel said in a post on X on Sunday that Addis Ababa was trying to create a pretext for attacking Eritrea.

images.caption: Sudanese, Eritrean, Egyptian and Somali leaders pose for a group photograph during the quadrilateral summit in New Alamein City, Egypt, on October 4, 2026 [Handout/Villa Somalia]

articles.title: Britain’s Green Party votes to class Zionism as a form of racism
articles.summary: Britain’s Green Party voted on Sunday to class Zionism as a form of racism, drawing criticism from British Jews and from the Israeli government which said it now viewed the party as “a body that gives legitimacy to terrorism.”
articles.body: Britain’s Green Party voted on Sunday to class Zionism as a form of racism, drawing criticism from British Jews and from the Israeli government which said it now viewed the party as “a body that gives legitimacy to terrorism.” The party – which received 6% of the vote in national elections in 2024 – said it regarded Zionism as “an ethnonationalist political project” and repeated its call for Britain’s Labour government to end all arms trade with Israel. “The motion also restates the Green Party’s backing for the right to self-determination and calls for the establishment of a single democratic state throughout historic Palestine,” the party said in a statement. The definition of Zionism – which inspired the foundation of the modern state of Israel in the 20th century – and what it implies for the rights of non-Jews in Israel and neighbouring territory, is contentious. Jewish groups sometimes define it as a right to Jewish self-determination. The Green Party motion passed by a majority of 1,022 to 813 despite opposition from many senior figures. Party leader Zack Polanski, who is seeking election to Parliament on Thursday in former Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s now-vacant London constituency, did not vote. The result was condemned by British Jewish groups. “The Green Party has made antisemitism party policy and become a racist party,” the Movement for Progressive Judaism said, adding that the support of some Jews for the motion did not mean it would not be used to discriminate against others. Israeli foreign minister Gideon Sa’ar has decided to declare Polanski barred from entering Israel, the foreign ministry said in a post on X Sunday. It said the Green Party motion “constitutes a clear antisemitic text according to the IHRA (International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance) definition, as it denies the Jewish people’s right to self-determination,” the ministry said. Mothin Ali, deputy leader of the Green Party and a supporter of the motion, told Sky News on Saturday that the heavy Palestinian death toll in Israel’s conflict with Hamas – which followed the Palestinian militant group’s deadly 2023 attack on an Israeli music festival – was the key context for the vote. “The motion defines Zionism quite clearly. It defines it as an ethnonationalist movement. It defines it as ethnic cleansing. It defines it as genocide,” Ali said. Britain’s government views Israeli settlers’ actions in the West Bank as amounting to ethnic cleansing but has said courts must decide if other Israeli actions qualify as genocide. Israel – which rejects claims of ethnic cleansing and genocide – called on Sunday for other British political parties to condemn the Green Party vote. “The Greens have adopted not only the green of Hamas, but also its ideology: the elimination of the State of Israel through armed struggle,” it said. Polanski and other senior Green Party figures said they would “continue to call out the heinous crimes of the Netanyahu government,” and that “there is no conflict between supporting the rights of Palestinians and the rights of Jewish people.”

articles.title: Singer Phil Collins blasts Trump as 'nasty,' teases song about America called 'Fat People with Guns'
articles.summary: Phil Collins revealed an unwritten song called "Fat People With Guns" about America and slammed Trump's demeanor in a "Piers Morgan Uncensored" interview.
articles.body: British rock icon Phil Collins took aim at President Donald Trump and revealed he has an unwritten song about America titled "Fat People With Guns" during a Friday "Piers Morgan Uncensored" interview, weeks before the musician is set to be included in the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame as a solo artist. After Morgan asked Collins directly what he thought of Trump, the 75-year-old musician said "not a lot" before criticizing the president’s demeanor and comparing him to past commanders in chief. "His whole manner is unattractive," he said. "Even when he's saying he did nothing. You know, I think that presidents – because historically, presidents have been eloquent and elegant... but you feel like even if you don't agree with them, you still respect them. But when someone like Trump is as nasty as he is, you end up feeling dislike for him." PHIL COLLINS GETS FRANK ON MARRIAGE FAILURES AND LIFE REGRETS: 'I REGRET MY MARRIAGES FALLING APART' Collins' remarks come amid a broader debate over musicians using their platforms to criticize Trump and the United States. Doug Eldridge, founder of Achilles PR, told Fox News Digital in June that criticism can take on a different meaning when artists move beyond individual politicians and target the country more broadly. "Outside of big city bubbles, most Americans really only care about elections during an election year; other than that, they have much bigger cares, concerns, and priorities," Eldridge said. "That changes; however, when the rhetoric shifts from party-specific, political criticism, to more broad statements about America, in general." "Artists with any regard for commercial appeal should ‘measure twice, cut once’ when disparaging American culture, character, and capability. The statement is free, but the response will prove costly." GOO GOO DOLLS' JOHN RZEZNIK DRAWS LINE ON POLITICS AT CONCERTS: 'I'M NOT GOING TO LECTURE YOU' Collins also took aim at the United States while discussing his songwriting process, revealing that he had saved a provocative phrase he could eventually develop into a song. "I've got a song that's waiting to be written called ‘Fat People with Guns,’ which is about America, you know, and I just write that phrase down so I don't forget it," Collins said. Sarah Schmidt, president of PR firm Interdependence, told Fox News Digital in June that artists can face backlash when audiences believe their political commentary has shifted toward criticism of Americans themselves. "If an artist mocks a USA chant from stage, they can face swift and intense backlash because it’s not them commenting on a politician or policy," she said. "It’s them criticizing the beliefs of the people who ultimately pay their bills." MICK JAGGER DOESN'T WANT TO 'LECTURE' FANS, SAYS HIS JOB IS TO MAKE PEOPLE 'HAVE THE BEST TIME' Collins also raised concerns about whether Trump could seek to stay in power beyond his second term, despite later describing himself as "not a political person." "I'm sure he's even tried, but it wouldn't surprise me if he just tries to overrule the two-term deal, you know, and American presidents can only serve two terms," he said. Trump appeared to shut down speculation about another run in August, telling reporters that the constitutional restriction on seeking another term was clear. articles.title: Ethiopia’s forces retake Mekelle amid renewed Tigray fighting
articles.summary: The capture of Tigray’s regional capital revives fears of another prolonged conflict, displacement and crisis.
articles.body:
Addis Ababa, Ethiopia – The capture of Tigray’s regional capital Mekelle by Ethiopian federal forces and allied Tigray Peace Force fighters has revived painful memories of the 2020–22 Tigray war, with residents fearing a return to prolonged violence, displacement and economic hardship.

The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) confirmed on Saturday that it had withdrawn from Mekelle, saying its regional administration would temporarily operate from another location. Government forces and allied fighters entered the city on Saturday, with a pro-government militia source, a humanitarian worker and a Mekelle resident confirming to the Reuters news agency on Sunday that they were in control of the city.

The development comes less than four years after the Ethiopian government and the TPLF signed the Pretoria agreement that ended two years of devastating fighting.

Berihu, a 32-year-old bajaj driver in Shire, northwestern Tigray, said the latest fighting had been particularly difficult to watch.

“I feel very heartbroken knowing that Tigray has gone back to full-scale war,” he said in a phone interview with Al Jazeera. “We have already seen what the last war did to our people, and now it feels like we are going through it all over again.”

The 2020–22 war killed hundreds of thousands of people, according to estimates, displaced millions and caused extensive damage to infrastructure and livelihoods.

The African Union-facilitated agreement, signed in Pretoria in November 2022, ended the large-scale fighting, but key issues, including the status of disputed territories, the return of displaced people and the disarmament of Tigrayan forces, remained unresolved.

In July, the TPLF said the Pretoria agreement had effectively collapsed, accusing the federal government of failing to implement key provisions. The federal government rejected that characterisation, saying it remained committed to the peace process while accusing the TPLF of undermining the agreement.

The political dispute was accompanied by growing military tensions, including reports of sporadic clashes and drone strikes in parts of Tigray. The two sides also traded accusations over troop movements and preparations for renewed fighting.

The capture of Mekelle marks a major development in the renewed conflict, putting the city once again at the centre of the fighting.

In Addis Ababa, the developments have also alarmed residents who remember the consequences of the previous war.

Abel, a 30-year-old shopkeeper, said the fighting had felt distant until explosions were heard in the capital .

“I woke up and heard that my city had been hit,” he said. “You hear about fighting in Tigray, and it feels far away. But when you hear about explosions in Addis Ababa, you start asking yourself what will happen next.”

Diplomatic sources said explosions were heard in several parts of the capital, including near the headquarters of Ethiopia’s military. Reuters separately reported that a source linked to an opposition alliance claimed the group had carried out drone strikes in Addis Ababa, including against military facilities. The claim could not be independently verified.

For Abel, the economic consequences are as concerning as the fighting itself.

“If the war becomes bigger, ordinary people will suffer,” he said.

Bisrat, a college student in Addis Ababa, said the overnight explosions had reinforced his fear that Ethiopia could be entering a much wider conflict.

“If Ethiopia goes into a full-scale war, ordinary people will suffer,” he said. “I fear seeing another Sudan.”

Sudan has been engulfed in war since April 2023, when fighting broke out between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, displacing millions and creating a major humanitarian crisis.

The current fighting also involves a wider set of actors than the Tigray war that ended in 2022. The TPLF is part of a broader opposition alliance that includes armed groups from several parts of the country.

Fighting has also spread into Afar, while relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea have sharply deteriorated.

Ethiopian officials have accused Eritrea of interfering in Ethiopia’s internal affairs and supporting forces opposed to the federal government. Eritrea has rejected the accusations.

On Thursday, Ethiopia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced the closure of its embassy in Asmara and declared 10 Eritrean diplomats persona non grata, saying they had been involved in activities that posed a threat to Ethiopia’s national security.

Eritrea subsequently announced that it was severing diplomatic relations with Ethiopia.

The diplomatic rupture has added to concerns that the renewed fighting could acquire a wider regional dimension.

In Mekelle, residents were left trying to understand what comes next after the TPLF withdrawal.

Goitom, 37, said there was a period of uncertainty after TPLF forces left the city, with what he described as a security vacuum allowing theft in some areas, including government offices.

“On Friday night, we were hearing gunfire but did not know what was happening,” he said.

By Saturday, Ethiopian federal forces and allied fighters had taken control of key locations, including the airport, according to Goitom. Reuters and The Associated Press news agency also reported that government-aligned forces had entered Mekelle following the TPLF withdrawal.

“It feels like we are back to square one,” he said. “We have already seen what war can do to this city and to our families. People are worried about what will happen next.”

The TPLF, however, portrayed the withdrawal as a tactical decision rather than an end to the fighting.

In a statement issued on Saturday, the group said it had “temporarily moved out of Mekelle” and that the regional government would “operate from somewhere else”. It said the decision was intended to prevent further destruction in the city and indicated that its forces would continue the conflict from other positions.

For the federal government, the capture of Mekelle represents a significant step towards restoring federal control over the region.

Abraham Belay, former president of the Tigray Interim Administration, said on Sunday that preparations were under way to establish a new interim administration in Tigray, with the aim of holding regional elections within months.

“We are working to establish a new administrative structure that will enable the people of Tigray to govern themselves,” Abraham said in an interview with Fana Broadcasting Corporate.

He said new administrative structures would be organised from the kebele level upwards, with community participation, before regional elections were held.

The competing accounts leave the next phase of the conflict uncertain. The federal government says it is seeking to restore its authority and establish a new regional administration, while the TPLF says its forces will continue fighting from elsewhere.

For people who lived through the previous war, the return of fighting has brought back fears of displacement, destruction and another prolonged humanitarian crisis.

Berihu, the bajaj driver, said he had seen villages bombed and civilians caught up in the fighting during the previous conflict, experiences that have shaped his fears about what could follow.

“It is painful to even think that civilians could once again bear the cost,” he said.

After years of displacement, loss and disruption, he said, many people in Tigray simply want the fighting to stop.

“We have already suffered enough,” Berihu said. “We just want peace. We don’t want to go through the same thing again.”

images.caption: Mekelle, Tigray’s regional capital, has been retaken by Ethiopian federal forces and allied fighters amid renewed fighting in the region [File: AFP]

articles.title: Nearly 1,500 migrants arrive in Myanmar from Malaysia despite UN warnings
articles.summary: Malaysia continues mass refugee deportations despite warnings from the UN about unsafe conditions in an active war zone.
articles.body:
Nearly 1,500 Myanmar refugees and migrants deported from Malaysia have arrived in their war-ravaged country under an opaque repatriation scheme heavily criticised by human rights groups and the United Nations refugee agency.

The 1,479 returnees, transported from Malaysia on board two navy warships and a hospital ship on Tuesday, arrived in southern Yangon early Sunday, Nay Lin Tun, a regional government minister, said.

They are among 5,000 Myanmar nationals who will be repatriated in stages from Malaysia, where more than 10,300 others are being held in immigration detention centres, according to the country’s Home Ministry.

Malaysia insists all returnees agreed to voluntary repatriation, but rights monitors have raised concerns that Myanmar refugees had little choice and warned that conditions for return remain unsafe.

The UN refugee agency said this past week that its staff were not allowed to meet the Myanmar nationals to confirm whether their decisions to return “were genuinely free and informed”.

Rohingya make up the majority of Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, but it remains unclear how many members of the persecuted Rohingya are among the returned group.

The deportation was carried out during escalating raids on refugee communities in Malaysia by immigration officials, which led to the detention of more than 50,000 refugees in 2026.

Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim announced the repatriations in July against a backdrop of rising xenophobia towards refugees, particularly the Rohingya.

Kuala Lumpur is moving ahead with plans to return a second group of more than 3,500 refugees and migrants, saying they have caused financial, social and security burdens.

While Malaysia is not a party to the UN Refugee Convention and treats refugees as undocumented migrants, it is home to about 215,600 refugees and asylum seekers registered with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).

This includes more than 126,000 mainly Muslim Rohingya refugees.

Myanmar pledged last month that returns will be “safe and dignified”.

But Yap Lay Sheng, a senior human rights specialist with Fortify Rights, told the AFP news agency: “There’s no telling how the regime would treat returnees.”

Myanmar has been accused of committing genocide against the Rohingya Muslim minority. Earlier this year, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) opened its first genocide case it has heard in full in more than a decade.

The UNHCR and rights groups said returnees could face persecution and forced military conscription in an active war zone. Myanmar has been embroiled in a civil war since the military seized power from the elected government in 2021.

The war has killed more than 100,000 people since the coup, according to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED) project.

Myanmar’s Min Aung Hlaing, the military coup leader who was installed as civilian president in April, is expected to visit Malaysia soon to discuss the repatriation scheme.

images.caption: A bus carrying Myanmar nationals being repatriated from Malaysia to the war-torn country heads towards the naval base in Lumut, on the outskirts of Kuala Lumpur, on September 29, 2026 [AFP]

articles.title: Brazil election: Lula, Flavio Bolsonaro head to runoff after tight first-round vote
articles.summary: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, an ally of US President Donald Trump and the eldest son of former president
articles.body: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, an ally of US President Donald Trump and the eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, will face each other in a runoff election on October 25 after neither secured the majority needed to win the presidency in the first round.Brazil's electoral authority said the 80-year-old Lula, who is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, and 45-year-old Bolsonaro advanced after finishing first and second in Sunday's vote.With more than 97% of ballots counted, Bolsonaro had 47.45% of valid votes, while Lula had 44.66%, according to Reuters.The electoral court in Brasilia earlier put Bolsonaro at just over 55.8 million votes and Lula at nearly 53.2 million. Both candidates were expected to address supporters.Cost of living, corruption and security dominate campaignThe two candidates will now have three weeks to appeal to voters who backed other candidates in the first round. The election campaign has focused on concerns over the rising cost of living, corruption and insecurity.Ronaldo Caiado and Renan Santos, who secured moderate support in Sunday's election, have previously said they would not endorse either candidate in the runoff, according to AP.Lula is expected to highlight his social policies and contrast them with Bolsonaro's political and legal background.His approval ratings have fallen during his third term, but he continues to retain support among voters who credit his social policies with improving the lives of millions of Brazilians, news agency AP reported.The incumbent also faces criticism over the country's affordability crisis and a corruption scandal involving the same Supreme Court justice who led the investigation into Jair Bolsonaro.Flavio Bolsonaro has campaigned on affordability and is expected to link Lula to corruption scandals. He has also promised tougher action against Brazilian criminal groups and called for better economic deals with the Trump administration, including in the rare-minerals sector.“Brazil needs change. Brazil can’t stand so much suffering,” Bolsonaro told reporters at a voting centre in Rio de Janeiro.He has also campaigned on securing the release of his father and bringing him back into politics.Lula and Bolsonaro offer contrasting foreign policy positionsThe runoff will also take place against a backdrop of tensions between Brazil and the Trump administration.Lula has accused the US administration of attempting to influence Brazil's election in Bolsonaro's favour through measures including tariffs, the revocation of the visa of Brazil's ambassador to Washington and sanctions against government officials and a Supreme Court justice.A Bolsonaro victory would increase US influence in Latin America, while a Lula victory would see Brazil maintain distance from Washington and continue deepening its relationship with China,.Trump allies have performed strongly in recent elections in Argentina, Colombia, Honduras and Peru.Voters divided over Bolsonaro and LulaBoth candidates face significant opposition among sections of the electorate. Roughly half of Brazil's population disapproves of the Bolsonaro family, while roughly half disapproves of Lula's Workers Party, according to multiple polls.Four years ago, Lula defeated Jair Bolsonaro by about 2.1 million votes.In Rio de Janeiro, Lula supporter and history professor Alvaro Senra, 65, said he was disappointed by the first-round result but believed Lula could still win.“I’m feeling calm but very sad with the result,” Senra said. “I think this is the result of conservatives working under the radar, including by neo-Pentecostal churches. But I think Lula can still win.”Maria Ribeiro, a 50-year-old cellphone vendor from Brasilia, said she voted for Flavio Bolsonaro because she wanted freedom to express her evangelical faith.“I voted for his father, and I don’t regret it,” she said.Lorena Zschaber, a 40-year-old photographer who watched the results at an LGBTQ+-friendly bar in Rio, said Bolsonaro's connection to his father concerned her.“I'm an LGBTQ+ woman, I can’t think of anything worse happening than Flávio Bolsonaro being elected,” she said.Rosângela Resende da Rocha, 69, said she supported Lula's social policies and his stance towards Trump.“That crazy guy wants to come in here to buy our country, so that our country will be like it is over there,” she said. “He won’t succeed if Lula wins.”Brazil's electronic voting system faces no major fraud findingBrazil's electronic voting system has not recorded any significant fraud since its adoption in the 1990s.The Organisation of American States' electoral observation mission said on Sunday that “the voting has been going smoothly and under adequate safety conditions”. Electoral authorities have said the electronic votes are secure and verifiable.“We are almost three hours away from the end of the voting and everything is proceeding normally and with the greatest possible transparency,” Superior Electoral Court president Kassio Nunes Marques said on Sunday afternoon. He added that there was “no concrete indication of international interference.”The next presidential term begins on January 5, 2027. The winner will lead Latin America's largest economy and a country with a population of about 214 million.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Trade: How India became dangerously addicted to Chinese imports
articles.summary: India’s toy shops provide an unlikely barometer by which to measure its economic relationship with China.
articles.body:
Take a walk into an Indian toy shop and as well as picking up a new favourite plaything for a child, you might just get an insight into how the nation is battling for a better economic relationship with its all-powerful neighbour China.

Six years ago, in an attempt to push local manufacturing and keep substandard toys out of its market, India raised tariffs on imported toys from 20% to 60% and eventually to 70%.

Retailers were up in arms and said that domestic firms could never match the foreign-made stuff. But the combination of higher customs duties and quality control standards worked.

Indian imports of toys fell by a third from nearly $300m (£227m) in 2020 to $100m this year, while exports rose from around $129m to $200m in the same period. Moreover, the country was able to drastically reduce its dependence on China, which held a 70% share of the local toy market.

The sector stands out as a rare exception in India's otherwise unsuccessful attempts to rebalance an increasingly lopsided trading relationship with its larger neighbour, which some experts say, is now among the most asymmetric in the world.

Even as diplomatic ties between the two countries completely broke down following the Galwan Valley clashes in 2020 and Delhi announced a slew of anti-dumping duties and a ban on Chinese apps such as Tik Tok, its trade deficit with Beijing has only ballooned - from $44bn in 2020 to an eye-popping $112bn this year.

"India's economic dependence on China continued to deepen while political, security, and investment ties were at their lowest point," Kevin Zongzhe Li, a Washington-based Fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute's Centre for China Analysis, told the BBC.

More worryingly, exports to China remained below pre-pandemic level even as imports doubled in this period.

"China now supplies over 30% of India's industrial imports, and India depends on it for more than 100 critical products. And the imbalance is worsening," says Ajay Srivastava of the Delhi-based Global Trade and Research Initiative (GTRI).

If the rapid pace of imports continues, bilateral deficit could jump to $134bn, giving Beijing even more leverage over Indian industry, according to Srivastava.

On the sidelines of the Brics summit in Delhi in September, amid a deepening thaw between the Asian giants, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping vowed to address these "structural trade imbalances and supply chain issues".

But given how deeply entrenched Chinese imports have become to India's industrial economy, this will be a formidable task for Delhi, experts told the BBC.

That's primarily because India depends on China to not merely consume end-products, but increasingly to produce industrial goods.

To be true, India has reduced its reliance on imports of finished goods such as smartphones and solar equipment, and now produces more than a quarter of the world's iPhones.

"Yet, production remains largely assembly-based and depends heavily on imported components, particularly from China," says Srivastava.

It's the same story with industrial machinery, battery inputs, chemicals, solar cells, and manufacturing equipment.

Electrical machinery and electronics alone account for 36% of imports, followed by machinery and mechanical appliances at 21.7%, while organic chemicals and plastics also have a significant share, according to the Observer Research Foundation (ORF) think tank.

"Their interruption would not merely affect consumption; it would disrupt production itself," according to Soumya Bhowmik, a Fellow at ORF's Centre for New Economic Diplomacy, who argues that this reflects India's difficulty in substituting Chinese inputs with local production.

Besides a growing reliance on inputs and raw material, Chinese imports to India are also being propelled by other macroeconomic trends.

China has huge excess capacity in sectors from steel to solar panels and electric vehicles, while its slowing economy cannot absorb the output.

Manufacturers are therefore increasingly turning to overseas markets, selling goods cheaply. China's trade surplus is expected to top $1tn for a second straight year.

A lot of these goods are coming to Indian shores because it is rapidly expanding manufacturing across segments of the economy, but also as "Western markets impose tariffs and other restrictions", says Srivastava.

On the other hand, lack of access to the Chinese market remains a major challenge for Indian companies.

"Indian products face a variety of tariff and non-tariff hurdles in China that make it difficult to scale exports," says Li.

"If normalisation [of ties] continues without a serious push for reciprocal market access, India risks a situation where the political relationship improves but the economic dependency stays the same."

The long term solution to both reducing avoidable imports and improving exports performance will be to strengthen manufacturing, says Srivastava.

But that requires sector-specific industrial policy and stronger fundamentals – affordable power and credit, efficient logistics and stable regulations – areas where India still falls short.

India has also recently softened foreign direct investment rules, which could open the door to Chinese companies wanting to expand Indian investments. But these too will need careful vetting, he adds.

"Investment that merely expands distribution networks or assembles products using Chinese parts could increase imports and deepen dependence. Approvals should therefore prioritise technology transfer, local value addition, domestic component production and exports from India."

More immediately, India could focus on targeting higher exports to China in specific sectors to reduce its trade asymmetry, says Li. Sectors like pharmaceuticals could be a natural fit with China's population aging and healthcare costs rising.

"But narrowing a $112bn deficit won't come from finding niche export sectors alone," he adds.

"The key question is whether Beijing is ready and willing to make concessions on market access as part of the broader normalisation. Alternatively, India will need to find its own leverage to force that conversation."

articles.title: Can the KKK find a new foothold in the US?
articles.summary: The infamous hate group is trying to rebrand itself as the ‘Knights Party’ in an attempt to grow its base.
articles.body:
Deleted: Experts have warned over the past decade of a resurgence in white supremacy in the United States, fuelled in part by the mainstream influence of political figures like President Donald Trump.

Just this year, the Public Religion Research Institute released the results of a 2025 survey that asked more than 20,000 US adults to evaluate the statement, “Immigrants are invading our country and replacing our cultural and ethnic background.”

That belief is the cornerstone of the great replacement theory , a conspiracy that falsely claims that immigrants, Jews and nonwhite groups seek to supplant white people in Western countries.

The research institute found that 32 percent of respondents – nearly one in three – nevertheless agreed with the idea.

Critics have accused right-wing leaders like Trump of normalising such views, through rhetoric that paints immigration as an “invasion” and “an assault on Western countries”.

Trump has also been accused of cosying up to white nationalists, even dining in 2022 with Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes, a key figure in the movement. When white nationalists engaged in a deadly clash with protesters in Charlottesville, Virginia, in 2017, Trump said there were “fine people on both sides”.

Al Jazeera correspondent Phil Lavelle travelled to Boone County, Arkansas, to see whether one of the most infamous white supremacist organisations in US history had seen a bump in its influence midway through Trump’s second term.

He spoke to Thomas Robb, the head of what was formerly known as the Knights of the Ku Klux Klan, a white supremacist group founded in the 1970s by David Duke.

What Lavelle found was a group seemingly eager to rebrand. The group had shortened its title to The Knights Party, and members told Lavelle they were trying to re-centre their message around family and faith.

But when Lavelle asked if a Black person would be welcome at the group’s church, Robb’s answer was simple.

“No,” Robb responded. “Because this is a white nationalist church.”

The Ku Klux Klan (KKK) has a long history of racism and violence in the US. The movement began at the end of the civil war in 1865, as a response to government efforts to expand civil rights to Black people and other minority groups.

Through lynchings and other targeted acts of violence, the KKK attempted to block non-white participation in government and maintain racial divides.

Robb, a Christian pastor, took over as the head of the Knights of the Ku Klux Klan – a faction of the KKK – in 1989. He has since attempted to broaden the group’s appeal.

He changed his title from “grand wizard” to “national director”, allowed new members to participate confidentially by mail, and distanced himself from KKK violence in public outreach campaigns.

Still, he has adhered to the racist philosophy his organisation is known for.

“What do you make of politicians like Zohran Mamdani or Abdul El-Sayed?” Lavelle asked Robb in his interview, referencing two high-profile US politicians who identify as Muslim.

“Well, first off, they’re not Americans,” Robb said. When Lavelle pointed out that El-Sayed was born in Michigan, Robb brushed off the contradiction. “I don’t care where he’s born. He’s not American.”

He proceeded to draw a distinction between the children of white and non-white immigrants. Only the children of white foreigners can be American, Robb said, “because they’re white”.

The Knights of the Ku Klux Klan is one of dozens of white supremacy organisations operating in the US.

The Southern Poverty Law Center, an advocacy group, estimates that there are at least 152 such groups active in the US today, part of what it calls a rising trend over the last decade.

Just this year, another white supremacist organisation, the Patriot Front, marched through Washington, DC , during the Independence Day holiday.

Critics say Trump, at times, has echoed their rhetoric. Trump told The New York Times earlier this year that “white people were very badly treated” in fields like academics.

He also instructed his second administration to dismantle diversity initiatives, and under his leadership, the government has launched probes into whether universities and companies like Nike discriminate against white people.

In addition, Trump has given priority to white South Africans in refugee admissions, falsely claiming they are the subject of a “genocide”.

Robb claimed the current rise in white nationalist sentiment began well before Trump, in 2008, during the election of Barack Obama, the country’s first Black president.

“People are beginning to stir and being angered by what they see happening to the country,” said Robb. “So we’re kind of a voice for that.”

Still, Robb acknowledged public wariness of joining a white supremacist group like his. “As for people actually to become members, that’s kind of a line they [are] a little hesitant to cross sometimes,” he said.

He also declined when asked to provide membership numbers or provide evidence for his assertion that support for his movement “is growing”.

“Maybe we’re wrong. Maybe everybody hates us. I don’t know,” Robb said.

articles.title: Brazil’s presidential race: Three key takeaways from the first round
articles.summary: Flavio Bolsonaro beat polling expectations as Brazil’s right gained ground, setting up October 25 run-off with Lula.
articles.body:
Brazil’s closely watched presidential election is heading to a second round between leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, prolonging a deeply polarised race with major implications for the country and the wider region.

Brazil’s electoral court confirmed on Sunday that the two candidates will advance to a run-off on October 25 after neither won the majority needed to secure the presidency outright, with Bolsonaro leading at 55.8 million votes to Lula’s almost 53.2 million.

Lula, 80, is seeking a fourth, non-consecutive term after a political career spanning nearly five decades.

Bolsonaro, 45, is the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro and is trying to return his father’s right-wing movement to power, even as the former president serves a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election.

The election comes at a pivotal time for Latin America’s largest economy. Brazilians are grappling with concerns over crime and the cost of living, while the country faces an increasingly tense relationship with the United States. The vote is also being closely watched across a region that has shifted sharply to the right in a series of recent elections.

While a second round was widely expected, the first-round result did not play out quite as pollsters had predicted.

Here are some of the key takeaways from the election so far.

Brazil is heading for another Lula-Bolsonaro run-off

With nearly 99 percent of votes reported, Bolsonaro had about 47 percent of valid votes, compared with 44.9 percent for Lula. Neither reached the 50 percent threshold needed to win in the first round.

That sets up another Lula-Bolsonaro showdown, four years after Lula narrowly defeated former President Jair Bolsonaro. This time, he will face the former president’s eldest son.

The race could be extremely close, as polling ahead of Sunday’s vote suggested Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro were roughly tied in a potential run-off.

That puts voters who backed one of the other 10 candidates in the first round at the centre of the fight for the presidency over the next three weeks.

Ronaldo Caiado and Renan Santos, who together received about 5.3 million votes, have previously said they will not endorse either candidate in the run-off.

Flavio Bolsonaro did better than polls suggested

Most polls leading up to election day predicted the race would be pushed into the second round, but had Lula finishing the first round ahead of Bolsonaro.

Instead, Bolsonaro emerged with a lead of two percentage points, raising questions about why the final polls underestimated his support.

On Sunday, Bolsonaro said the results showed that Brazilians want change.

Analysts told the Reuters news agency that Bolsonaro may have benefitted from “protest votes” from people who may have preferred another candidate but saw defeating Lula as the priority. Many had been expected to shift their support to Bolsonaro only in a second round, meaning this could have consequences for his support in three weeks.

“The protest vote foreshadows what is to come in the run-off,” political analyst Rafael Favetti told Reuters. “While this should benefit Flavio Bolsonaro now, his growth potential in the second round drops precisely because that support has already been front-loaded.”

After the results came in, Lula said the votes were “unexpected” but that he would come back stronger in the run-off.

“I admit, I was convinced I would win in the first round. The game is about to start. We are in extra time. In extra time, we will win over the Brazilian people,” the 80-year-old said.

Bolsonaro’s surprising performance in the first round was part of a broader show of strength for Brazil’s right.

Right-wing parties, led by Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party (PL), were performing strongly in both houses of Congress, with the PL on track to emerge as the largest force in the Chamber of Deputies and making gains in the Senate.

This included victories for other members of the Bolsonaro family , including former First Lady Michelle Bolsonaro, Flavio’s stepmother, who won a Senate seat in the Federal District, her first elected office.

His brother, Carlos Bolsonaro, was elected to the Senate in Santa Catarina.

The results show that the political movement built around former President Jair Bolsonaro – known as “bolsonarista” – remains a powerful electoral force, even with the former president barred from running himself.

“The fact that far-right candidates for the legislature have exceeded all expectations suggests a deeper popular grounding for the bolsonarista project than many expected,” Andre Pagliarini, an assistant professor of history and international studies at Louisiana State University and author of a book on Lula, told Al Jazeera.

“Millions of Brazilians right now evidently feel the right best reflects their values and vision for the future,” he added.

The congressional results matter beyond election night, too. Both houses were already dominated by conservative lawmakers, and a stronger right-wing presence could make it even harder for Lula to push through his agenda if he wins another term.

A Bolsonaro victory, meanwhile, could give him more room to pursue his own priorities, including his pledge to seek an amnesty for his father.

articles.title: US coastguard suspends search for six on board crashed medical jet
articles.summary: Debris found off Nantucket island after the air ambulance disappeared while flying from Bermuda to Boston.
articles.body:
The United States coastguard has suspended its search for six people on board a medical transport jet that crashed while flying from Bermuda to Boston.

“Suspending a search is not an easy decision,” Rear Admiral Matthew Lake, commander of the ⁠coastguard’s Northeast District, said in a statement on Sunday.

The search was called off after teams spent about 66 hours covering 4,445 miles (7,150km) by air and sea and confirmed that debris found off the shore of Massachusetts’s Nantucket Island came from the aircraft.

The Gulfstream G100 carried two pilots, two medical staff, a patient and a relative, Clarence Togeretz, director of flight operations at Canada-based Latitude Air Ambulance, told Canada’s public broadcaster CBC.

The four crew members were Canadian, and the two passengers were Bermudian, according to authorities.

In a statement on Sunday, Latitude Air Ambulance said, “Given the information shared by authorities and the conclusion of ⁠the search-and-rescue phase, we must now face the heartbreaking reality that the four members of our Latitude team, our patient and the patient’s family escort, who were ⁠aboard Heartbeat 104, are presumed to have died.”

Attention has turned to what happened in the jet’s final minutes, when flight-tracking data showed a steep descent and air traffic controllers struggled to re-establish contact.

Authorities have not determined what caused the aircraft to come down.

The aircraft had flown to Bermuda to collect the patient and was heading to Boston Logan International airport.

The US Federal Aviation Administration alerted the coastguard at about 2am on Saturday (06:00 GMT) after contact with the jet was lost.

Lake said at a Sunday news conference that the water around the debris was about 80 to 90 feet (24-27 metres) deep.

He offered condolences to the families of those on board and thanked the agencies involved in the operation.

Latitude Air Ambulance specialises in medical evacuation and repatriation flights, carrying patients home from other countries.

The company says its missions are normally staffed by two pilots and medical personnel.

articles.title: All passengers presumed dead after plane went missing off US coast
articles.summary: The aircraft lost communication with flight controllers after significantly dropping in altitude, according to flight data.
articles.body:
Six people aboard a medical transport aircraft that went missing on Saturday while it was travelling from Bermuda to Boston are presumed dead, according to a statement from the flight's operator.

On Sunday evening, the United States Coast Guard said it was ending its search for survivors off the coast of Nantucket, a Massachusetts island.

"We must now face the heartbreaking reality that the four members of our Latitude team, our patient and the patient's family escort, who were aboard Heartbeat 104, are presumed to have died," Latitude Air Ambulance said in a statement shortly thereafter.

"Our thoughts are first and foremost with their families, loved ones, friends, and colleagues."

The Federal Aviation Administration lost contact with the Gulfstream G-100 plane just after 01:00 local time (05:00 GMT) on Saturday morning.

On Saturday evening, authorities located a "debris field" confirmed to be from the aircraft.

The plane had departed from Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport at 23:40 local time on Friday night, according to flight data from FlightAware, and was due to land at Boston's Logan International at 01:30 EDT (05:30 GMT).

Four Canadian nationals and two Bermudian nationals were onboard.

"This is an unimaginable loss for our Latitude family and for everyone who loved the six people aboard Heartbeat 104," said Peter Byl, President of Latitude Air Ambulance, on Sunday evening.

"Our focus now is on supporting their families, supporting our people and assisting the authorities. We will honour our colleagues by remembering the care, professionalism, and commitment they brought to their work every day."

Latitude Air Ambulance is a Canadian company that provides international medical flights for patients returning home.

Two pilots and two medical staff, both Canadian, had flown to Bermuda to collect a patient and their relative, Clarence Togeretz, director of flight operations at Latitude, told CBC News.

FlightAware's tracker shows that the aircraft significantly dropped in altitude before its communications went dark, plummeting from around 7,300m (24,000ft) to 3,300m (11,000ft).

Radio transmissions show trouble with communications between the air traffic controller and the pilot, the Boston Globe reported, based on transmissions provided by LiveATC.net.

"You're coming in blind? Is that what you said?" the air traffic controller asked. "Are you declaring an emergency, or no?"

"You're coming in a little weak so I didn't hear what your response was, if you were declaring an emergency or not," the air traffic controller said, according to the Globe.

The air traffic controller later confirmed the pilot had declared an emergency.

An area fire dispatcher asked emergency crews just after 01:00 EDT to prepare to meet a plane with an "electrical issue".

The dispatcher later said "the aircraft has lost radio and radar".

Latitude said in its statement on Sunday evening that it would continue to cooperate with relevant authorities during ongoing recovery efforts and investigations.

"Determining the circumstances and cause of an aviation accident is a careful and methodical process, and we will not speculate about what occurred," the company said.
