articles.title: Potty-training scheme to expand to more parts of England after city's success
articles.summary: The government wants 75% of children to end their first year of school with a good level of development by 2028.
articles.body:
The number of children who were toilet-trained before starting school this year has increased significantly in a city where parents were given potty training guides with their first school offers.

York was the subject of the city-wide pilot, which also put on workshops for parents and offered special training for early years staff.

Twenty local authorities across England are now signed up to launch similar schemes to tackle the number of pupils starting school without being fully toilet-trained.

The government said the pilot's results were "encouraging", and confirmed they were committed to 75% of pupils reaching a good level of development at the end of their first year in school by 2028.

Since April this year, parents across York have been targeted via GP surgeries, pharmacies, family hubs, schools and nurseries with information and offers of support on how to potty-train their child ahead of starting school.

Potty training guides were sent out to all families across York who had a child starting reception in September - with the aim that all children could use the toilet independently by the time they started school, except those with medical issues or special educational needs.

The results from all 55 mainstream primary schools across the city, shared exclusively with BBC News, suggested there had been a 43% drop since last year in the number of children who were not fully toilet-trained when they started school.

Across York last September, 148 out of 1,364 reception pupils (11%) were recorded as not being toilet-trained when they started school. This year, that fell to 85 reception pupils out of 1,374 (6%).

Parents Natalie and Lucy, who both have daughters starting reception next year, have welcomed the extra support on offer.

Lucy said she had noticed the drop-in sessions on potty training in her local children's centre and thought it was a "really good idea".

"I think it's really important that children are more prepared for that aspect of starting school," she said.

Natalie said getting her daughter Freya potty-trained in time for school has been a priority, but feels there is a lot of pressure on parents to do so.

"I think going to school is hard enough for children," she said.

"But for me it was really important that she's confident enough to use toilets, to be independent, to be able to go without relying on the help of teachers perhaps in an environment where they've already got lots of children to look after."

Natalie said the popularity of disposable nappies might be a reason why parents often wait longer to potty train.

"When I was little, we still had the terry towelling nappies and they had to be washed and hung on the line. So I think with disposable nappies it's easier," she said.

Around one in four children started school in England and Wales last year not fully toilet-trained, and teachers said they have been spending over an hour a day changing nappies, according to the latest research from the children's charity Kindred Squared .

Jo Mould, who teaches reception at Robert Wilkinson Primary Academy in York, said she has noticed an improvement in pupils being ready for school this year.

"We've spent more time teaching in these last three weeks than we have in previous years," she said.

"The children have come in so ready to learn, because they're more settled and regulated socially and emotionally. We've had a really, really positive start to the school year."

York councillor Bob Webb said the impact of the scheme had been "so positive" for both schools and families.

But he acknowledged a potential "gap in support" for parents between seeing health visitors with their toddler, and the child later arriving at school.

He said the key to the scheme's success was collaboration across health visitors, schools and other community settings, but that there was "always more that could be done at an earlier age".

Twenty local authorities across England have now committed to adopt York's model, developed by Kindred Squared, and use it to encourage earlier potty-training in their areas.

Just over two-thirds of children in England (68.3%) leave reception class with a good level of development - a key measure of school readiness which includes things like communication skills, as well as physical, social and emotional development - according to the latest government stats .

That means they were assessed by teachers on being able to complete tasks like going to the toilet and paying attention in class.

The government has said it is still committed to increasing that proportion to 75% by 2028.

Early Education Minister Paul Waugh said it was "encouraging to see this pilot helping more children develop the confidence and independence they need before starting school", stressing the importance of parents taking early steps towards toilet training.

In York, Mould said she hopes next year's parents will take on potty-training even earlier.

"Ideally we'd be at the point where [children] don't need that support when they get here, because they've already been trained by the time they get to us."

articles.title: Russia's pneumonic plague scare: Nearly 200 quarantined after lab worker's death - all you need to know
articles.summary: Nearly 200 people have been placed under medical observation in Russia's Irkutsk region after a laboratory worker died following severe pneumonia, with
articles.body: Nearly 200 people have been placed under medical observation in Russia's Irkutsk region after a laboratory worker died following severe pneumonia, with reports suggesting she may have contracted plague at a research facility in Siberia. Russian authorities, however, have not publicly confirmed that the woman died from pneumonic plague and have described the illness as a “particularly dangerous infection” and pneumonia of “unknown aetiology”.The case involves an researcher of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Shelekhov, near the regional capital Irkutsk, according to Russian state-run news agency TASS and reports cited by CNN.According to reports, the 27 or 28-year-old laboratory worker was admitted to a hospital in Shelekhov on Tuesday with severe pneumonia. She was placed on a ventilator and died on Thursday, according to reports cited by The Moscow Times.Reports said the woman may have accidentally broken a test tube containing live bacteria while collecting samples for testing. The circumstances of the alleged laboratory incident have not been independently confirmed.What Russian authorities have saidRussia's federal consumer and health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said the worker had been diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown aetiology”, indicating that the exact cause of the illness had not been established.According to CNN, Rospotrebnadzor said “the sanitary and epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk region, the cities of Irkutsk and Shelekhov is stable”.The agency said it had introduced specialised measures “in connection with the case of an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute”.Alexei Tsydenov, head of neighbouring Buryatia, said the woman had died from an unspecified form of plague, according to The Moscow Times. Earlier reports cited by CNN said Tsydenov described the possibility that she had died “possibly from the plague”.At the same time, Tsydenov stressed that “There are no plague outbreaks in the republic, including in areas bordering Mongolia”.Irkutsk governor Igor Kobzev also urged residents to remain calm after an emergency meeting involving regional authorities and Russia's chief state medical officer.According to CNN, Kobzev described the meeting as being linked to a “suspected case of a particularly dangerous infection affecting a resident of the region”.Nearly 200 people under observationAuthorities have stepped up precautionary measures around Shelekhov following the worker's death.According to reports cited by The Moscow Times, at least 197 people who may have come into contact with the woman were placed under medical observation, with more than 100 reportedly in hospital wards.The Shelekhov district hospital was also placed under quarantine while a special commission assessed the situation. Reports also said isolation measures were introduced at at least one maternity facility in the municipality.An aluminium plant located near the research facility instructed employees to wear face coverings.Artem Fominikh, head of the Irkutsk Aluminium Plant, urged people to remain calm amid speculation, saying according to CNN that “there are many rumours and conflicting reports circulating”.“All identified close contacts are under medical supervision. At present, they show no signs of the disease, and their laboratory test results are negative,” Fominikh said, according to CNN.Kobzev similarly said on Telegram that “All identified contact persons have been placed under medical observation. As of today, the contacts show no signs of illness, and their laboratory test results are negative,” according to The Moscow Times.Authorities also reportedly cancelled planned public events in Irkutsk, while law enforcement opened a criminal investigation into possible violations of health and safety rules resulting in death.Is it pneumonic plague?The exact nature of the infection remains unclear based on the information released publicly by Russian authorities.Media reports have described the case as suspected pneumonic plague, while official statements cited by CNN have referred to pneumonia of unknown origin and a suspected particularly dangerous infection.Gennady Onishchenko, the former head of Rospotrebnadzor, said the pathogen was “most likely not the plague”. He also said that even if plague were confirmed, “there will be no spread of this disease”.Pneumonic plague is one of the three main forms of plague caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. Unlike bubonic plague, which is commonly associated with infected fleas and animals, pneumonic plague affects the lungs and can spread from person to person through respiratory droplets, according to information cited by CNN and the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.Symptoms can include fever, headache and weakness, followed by rapidly developing pneumonia, breathing difficulties, chest pain, coughing and, in some cases, bloody or watery sputum, according to the CDC information cited in the reports.US monitoring suspected caseThe United States is also monitoring reports of the suspected fatal case, according to a State Department official cited by Fox News.The official said Washington was aware of reports of a death in Irkutsk Oblast and was following the situation in coordination with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and other federal agencies.The official stressed that many details remained unconfirmed and urged Russian authorities to provide accurate information quickly.Former CIA officer Dan Hoffman told Fox News Digital that the US intelligence community was likely collecting information from multiple sources about the incident.“I would also expect our embassy in Moscow to be engaging with their diplomatic counterparts at an official level because we might have people in Russia who might be at risk,” Hoffman said.“Washington will be speaking to all of our allies and partners in the region and sharing what we know.”The State Department official said pneumonic plague can be treated with antibiotics, particularly when treatment begins early, according to Fox News. The CDC recommends starting appropriate treatment as soon as plague is suspected.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Imran Khan: Supporters of jailed ex-PM march to Pakistan capital
articles.summary: Thousands have taken to the streets after talks between authorities and Khan's party ended in deadlock.
articles.body:
Thousands of supporters of Pakistan's jailed ex-prime minister Imran Khan are marching to the capital Islamabad as they call for his release.

Concerns over the 73-year-old's health have grown louder in recent months. His family claims he has lost most of his vision in his right eye after prison authorities failed to take action.

The cricket star-turned-politician, who faces charges in more than 100 cases, was jailed for 17 years over corruption last year. Khan said all the cases against him are politically motivated.

Even behind bars, he remains a force in Pakistani politics, and demonstrations in support for him have led to deadly violence and crackdowns in the past.

Sunday's march, which began in Lakki Marwat, a city 275km away from Islamabad, had paused for the night and is expected to resume around midday local time on Monday.

Originally scheduled for last week, it was postponed to allow for talks between the government and Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party but the talks ended in a deadlock.

Khan, who faces charges ranging from leaking state secrets to selling state gifts, was first imprisoned in August 2023. His wife Bushra Bibi was jailed along with him last year.

Sohail Afridi, chief minister for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province ruled by PTI, expects that the march will make its way to a town about 80km (50 miles) west of Islamabad by Thursday.

"[By then] this movement will have reached every corner of the country and every square will have become a centre of activity," he said on Sunday, urging the people to "play an active role in the political process".

Authorities in Islamabad have stacked up shipping containers to block key access routes to the capital city.

The PTI said talks with government failed because authorities rejected the party's request for access to Khan so that its leaders could consult him on national and political issues.

The party also said it had demanded that Khan be given an immediate medical examination and treatment.

Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi meanwhile accused Afridi of "sabotaging" negotiations, saying the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government had backed out of earlier commitments on counter-terrorism issues, according to Pakistan's local media reports.

In August, Khan was briefly transferred from jail to a state-run hospital for medical examination and treatment following complaints about his deteriorating health. The doctors later deemed him "medically fit".

The intervention was the most significant relief Khan has received from the courts since he was imprisoned in 2023 on corruption charges, which he says were politically motivated.

Khan's family and the PTI, however, criticised the authorities for defying a court order that he be examined by physicians at a specific private hospital.

On 20 September, Khan's sister Aleema Khanum was arrested in the eastern city of Lahore.

The arrest order said Khanum had been mobilising people to "create law and order situations" and "raising/chanting objectionable slogans amongst the general public against the Government".

Khan, who previously captained the Pakistan national cricket team, served as the country's prime minister from 2018 to 2022.

His arrest in May 2023 sparked large-scale, violent protests by supporters, who ransacked the corps commander's residence in Lahore, smashing chandeliers and making away with furniture, paintings, and even peacocks, among other things.

At least eight people died in the protests and the army had to be called in to quell the violence.

Former international cricket captains have made several appeals in recent months to Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif urging Khan be accorded proper medical care.

articles.title: Cornell student who gave police leads in alleged rape says she feels ‘betrayed’ over its handling
articles.summary: The student said she spoke with campus police in 2024 with what she believed was useful information about what was alleged at the Chi Phi fraternity house.
articles.body: A Cornell University student gave campus police leads in the alleged rape of Jane Doe in 2024 but expressed dismay over how the authorities handled the case. The student, who spoke to NBC News on Sunday on condition of anonymity over concerns about repercussions, said she first heard about allegations that Doe was raped as a rumor on campus about 24 to 48 hours after the incident. Doe, who filed a lawsuit last month, claimed she was plied with alcohol and ketamine and gang-raped at the Chi Phi fraternity house the night of Oct. 19-20. The student recalled rumors that Doe was planning to have a threesome but that it had “gone off the rails,” and she remembers being “really horrified by it.” “From that night, I think, we just kind of started, like, hearing more,” the student said. Talk of the alleged sexual assault became widespread on campus after the school issued a crime safety alert about a report of a sexual assault at a fraternity. “The thing I think we all feel, like, betrayed in regards to is that, like, it wasn’t handled,” she said. “When we got the police report, I think we all assumed it was being, you know, it would be, like, handled properly, yeah, and it was, like, in good hands.” The student, who discussed details corroborated by documents reviewed by NBC News, said she and a friend initially gave a tip to authorities after the crime alert was issued. Police later called her and asked her to come in and speak with them days after Doe reported the incident to Cornell police on Nov. 8. The student said she decided to go to police after she saw screenshots of a Chi Phi group message on Snapchat and because “it felt like the right thing to do if we could help this girl.” Doe’s lawsuit included a screenshot of a Chi Phi Snapchat group message that said there was “free p----” in a room in the frat house where Doe was the night she alleges she was assaulted. “That was, like, when I kind of internally made the decision. OK, like, I’m taking this all in, and then I’m going to the police tomorrow,” the student said. She recalled sitting with one or two officers for about half an hour during her interview with police. “They seemed fairly competent. It seemed like a normal interview process to me,” she said. She said she walked them through everything she knew, including that fraternity members were messaging about the events of that evening with Doe and about potential witnesses. She also gave police secondhand information about drug use at Chi Phi and said she is familiar with the frat house and believed she knew where ketamine was alleged to be kept. “I guess I assumed that, like, I wasn’t enough,” the student said. Cornell did not immediately respond to a request for comment Sunday on the student’s account to police. In a video statement Saturday, President Michael I. Kotlikoff called the allegations “deeply disturbing” and said they raise questions about the investigations that were conducted. He said he welcomes an independent review of how the university handled the matter, which will be conducted by an outside law firm. Police records obtained by NBC News showed that Cornell police spoke to multiple witnesses and fielded anonymous tips about the allegations of a gang rape at the fraternity house — but that the information was not referred to the local prosecutor for review in his deciding whether to bring charges. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten told NBC News on Friday that the interviews that were flagged “were each of the frat members declining to speak on the advice of their attorney.” He did not respond to a follow-up request asking whether he was told about interviews with other fraternity members in addition to tips from callers. Van Houten ultimately determined the allegations did not warrant charges because of a lack of criminality. Doe’s suit has sparked uproar and criticism of Cornell and Van Houten’s handling of her allegations. Van Houten has since agreed to reopen his inquiry into Doe’s allegations, but New York Gov. Kathy Hochul last week named state Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor in the matter. The student who spoke with campus police criticized how the department handled the matter. While students believed there was an active investigation into Doe’s claims, people continued going to Chi Phi, including the room at the center of the allegations. Within Greek life at Cornell, “rumors spread fast,” the student said, and even if you did not know Doe or the men, “you knew someone who did.” Doe’s lawsuit named Cornell, Chi Phi and the seven fraternity brothers among the defendants. None of the seven has been criminally charged. The fraternity was suspended from campus, and it remains barred. Cornell said in a statement Sept. 28 that it conducted a thorough, monthslong Title IX investigation that handed down “a range of sanctions which included expulsions and suspensions” from the university. Attorneys for two of the seven men have denied to NBC News that they sexually assaulted Doe. An attorney for a third man denied the allegations to ABC News. NBC News has not received responses to requests for comment from the five other men. Chi Phi’s national fraternity condemned sexual assault and drug and alcohol abuse in a statement Wednesday. It said that the fraternity members Doe named were kicked out of the organization and that the national fraternity permanently expelled the chapter. “At every level of Chi Phi, we will take steps like these whenever they are needed to protect the integrity of our fraternity and the safety of our communities,” said Trey Robb, the national fraternity’s interim executive director. Some of the men faced backlash as talk spread on campus. Two of the Chi Phi brothers named in the suit were kicked out of their rugby club after the allegations came to light, a former teammate told NBC News. “We kicked [them] off the team immediately before the school expelled them,” said the teammate, who requested anonymity because of the sensitivity of the matter. The teammate said he has participated in discussions among a group of current and former rugby players about responding publicly to Doe’s lawsuit. “As a team, it was important for us to support this victim,” he said. “We are extremely, extremely distraught.” Cornell Rugby said in a statement that it was “deeply disturbed” by the allegations and that its thoughts were with Doe. “Players who were known to be connected with the alleged events were permanently removed from the team and alumni network as soon as their affiliation with the incident was established,” it said. No current members of the team have been affiliated with Chi Phi, the statement said. As news of the allegations spread, some discussions were supportive of Doe, but others shamed her in conversations, a former member of Doe’s sorority, Delta Delta Delta, told NBC News. “Some people were sympathizing with Jane Doe, but also, people didn’t know details,” said the former member, who has graduated and requested anonymity out of a concern for privacy. Another student and former member of Tri Delta told NBC News that she recalled learning about the incident through rumors and described the student body as “really pissed off about it.” That student said that she was at the same sorority-hosted event the evening of Oct. 19 that Doe attended and which was referred to in her lawsuit but that Doe disappeared during the evening. A few days later, the student said, Doe said people were spreading rumors about her and she was not sure what to make of it, “and it just seemed like everybody was very confused at the moment.” A third former Tri Delta member told NBC News that the campus learned of the incident from the university alert and described students feeling “shock” and “really appalled.” She, too, is critical of how Cornell handled the matter. “I think that shows a lack of respect for their female students and kind of makes it less enticing to attend the university,” she said. Today, within the sorority there is a resounding wave of support for Doe, she said, as well as “frustration and anger.” Tri Delta said in a statement on behalf of its national organization and its Cornell chapter, “As an organization, we are committed to supporting women and victims of sexual violence.” If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-4673. The hotline, run by the Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network (RAINN), can put you in contact with your local rape crisis center. You can also access RAINN’s online chat service at

articles.title: A schoolteacher's 128-acre family retreat became part of a larger wildlife corridor; decades after buying the land, Jeanne Paisley's conservation easement now protects forests, wetlands and a stream linked to the Chesapeake watershed
articles.summary: When life doesn't give you time to breathe, you tend to look out for space to do the same yourself, deliberately.
articles.body: When life doesn't give you time to breathe, you tend to look out for space to do the same yourself, deliberately. For Jeanne Paisley, a schoolteacher with three kids and a half-hour daily commute, there was a consistent wish for some room to breathe. According to The Land Steward, the Spring 2013 newsletter of the Finger Lakes Land Trust, Paisley had bought 128 acres of forests, fields and wetlands in the town of Richford in Tioga County, New York.A campsite she couldn't forgetIt all began with a family road trip. Paisley and her husband lived on Long Island and had no summer work. Thus, the couple decided to buy a tent and took their three children on a trip all over the United States and Canada. When they returned to New York, they chanced upon this land and the family agreed it was the best campsite they had ever seen.The land suited her job as well. The drive to Paisley's school was just half an hour and she liked the setting. She recalled seeing red salamanders in the driveway when they first arrived at the site. And what made her especially glad was that there, no neighbour would ask her to mow her lawn. For her, the appeal was natural beauty and the freedom to leave nature alone.Paisley traced her love for the outdoors to her childhood during the Great Depression. When her father was unemployed, the family moved to the country. They built a small house and carried spring water up the hill. That early life stayed with her. In her words, "Caring about nature is just part of how I think." She added that she always knew she wanted to protect the land at some point. Decades later, she did just that.A protected forestAbout 40 years later, at the age of 86, Paisley still continued to reside on the land. She had placed a conservation easement on her property with the Finger Lakes Land Trust. A conservation easement is an agreement that restricts the manner in which the land will be developed in the future.In this case, it was aimed at protecting the mature forests and prime farmland in the area of the east branch of Owego Creek. The Land Trust noted that two attorneys, John Alexander and Eric Haselbauer, provided pro bono legal help. This protection mattered because it helps safeguard the watershed. As reported in The Land Steward, David Diaz, the Land Trust's director of land protection, said the property helps maintain local watershed quality and supports fish such as eastern brook trout. He explains that because of its steep slopes and presence of a seasonal stream, the land is particularly susceptible to erosion due to stormwater runoff if disturbed by future development. Such damage can affect the water quality not only of the Owego Creek but also of waters many miles downstream. The property lies in a focus area for the Land Trust, where tributaries flow into the Upper Susquehanna River. That river's watershed drains into the Chesapeake Bay, the country's largest estuary.Andy Zepp, executive director of the Land Trust, said she and her family helped expand a network of protected lands in her Southern Tier neighbourhood. Her property joins several nearby protected areas, including multiple state forests, the Land Trust's King Nature Preserve, and another conservation easement.In a 2019 review published in Science Advances, Gregory Bratman and his co-authors summarise research related to nature and its impacts on mental health. Time spent in nature, the researchers argue, is linked with better well-being, better sleep, and lower stress. Many of the findings show links, not proof. Experiments suggest a short time in nature can brighten mood, but it is less clear whether that builds long-term mental health. The paper also lists water purification as one example of the benefits ecosystems provide, echoing Diaz's point about water quality at Owego Creek.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: October 5, 1892 heist: The Dalton Gang tried to rob two banks at once in broad daylight, but a cashier stalled them, townspeople grabbed guns and the daring heist ended in a deadly shootout
articles.summary: Five men rode into Coffeyville, Kansas, on horseback on a bright October morning in 1892.
articles.body: Five men rode into Coffeyville, Kansas, on horseback on a bright October morning in 1892. They had come to do something no other gang had managed before: rob two banks at exactly the same time.The plan sounded almost absurdly confident. Bob and Emmett Dalton would enter the First National Bank. Grat Dalton, Dick Broadwell and Bill Powers would hit the Condon Bank across the street. The men knew Coffeyville well. The Dalton brothers had lived there before becoming outlaws.They also believed they could get in, take the money and disappear before anyone understood what had happened. Instead, within minutes, the town was armed.And by the time the shooting stopped, four members of the gang were dead, four local men had also been killed, and the fifth Dalton brother involved in the robbery, Emmett, was badly wounded.The plan was bigger than a normal bank robberyThe Dalton Gang had already built a reputation across the American West.For about a year and a half, according to History.com, the gang had been involved in train robberies and other crimes. The website notes that the group had managed to avoid capture despite efforts by law officers.But the Daltons apparently wanted one final spectacular score.History.com describes their October 5 attempt as a “daring daylight robbery” of two Coffeyville banks at the same time.The choice of Coffeyville was not random. It was familiar territory for the Dalton brothers. They knew the town and its streets, and they knew where the two banks stood.Their plan depended on speed. They would split into two groups, enter the banks simultaneously, take the money and get back to their horses.But there was a problem they could not control. People noticed them.One mistake gave the town time to reactThe gang rode into town and left their horses in an alley near the banks. They then split up. Bob and Emmett went into the First National Bank. Grat, Broadwell and Powers entered the Condon Bank.The robbery initially appeared to be going according to plan. Then someone recognised one of the men. The warning began spreading through Coffeyville. And ordinary townspeople started reaching for guns.While Bob and Emmett were putting money into a grain sack, “the townspeople ran for their guns” and surrounded the banks. That detail changes the entire picture of the robbery.The Daltons had imagined themselves controlling the situation because they were armed and had planned the attack carefully. However, the people outside were waiting.Inside the other bank, a cashier bought precious minutesThe most unusual part of the story happened at the Condon Bank. Grat Dalton, Broadwell and Powers demanded access to the vault. The cashier, Charles Ballard, knew that giving them the money immediately could put everyone in greater danger. So he stalled.He told the robbers that the vault was on a time lock and could not be opened yet.According to the Coffeyville Historical Society, the men arrived at around 9:20 a.m., and the cashier's claim bought the town valuable time while people armed themselves.Then the shooting startedWhen the Dalton brothers came out of the First National Bank, gunfire erupted. They were forced back inside. They tried to escape through the rear, but townspeople were waiting there too. Across the street, Broadwell, Powers and Grat Dalton also found themselves trapped. The situation quickly became a gun battle between the gang and armed Coffeyville residents.The town's defenders weren't professional soldiers. They were shopkeepers, workers and other local men who had decided they weren't going to let the robbery happen without a fight.Four gang members diedBob Dalton was killed. So were his brother Grat, Bill Powers and Dick Broadwell. Emmett Dalton was shot more than 20 times but survived.Four Coffeyville defenders were killed: Marshal Charles T. Connelly, Lucius Baldwin, George Cubine and Charles Brown. Several others were wounded.So although the story is often remembered as a spectacular failure by a gang of outlaws, it was also a deadly confrontation that left families in the town grieving.You use AI every day. articles.title: Panto return planned for Raac-affected Orchard Theatre
articles.summary: The council says the refurbishment of the Dartford venue has cost nearly £30m.
articles.body:
A Kent theatre which closed over fears of dangerous concrete say it is confident the venue will reopen in time for this year's pantomime season.

The Orchard Theatre in Dartford shut in September 2023 after reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete (Raac) was found in its roof.

It had been due to reopen in May 2025, but the date was pushed back after Dartford Borough Council identified further essential work needed to meet safety requirements .

Jeremy Kite, leader of the council, said much of the work over the past three years had focused on replacing the roof and flooring.

"When the theatre had to be closed three years ago, it was one of the worst days of my life," he recalled.

Kite added decades of wear and tear, changing technology, new regulations and the need for major structural improvements had all contributed to the scale of the project, which has cost almost £30m.

"Theatres are expensive buildings," he says. "But we're determined to keep it because of the important role it plays in the community."

During the closure, the council set up a temporary theatre to ensure performances could continue.

Kite added the theatre would reopen in time for Cinderella performances starting on 12 December.

"This building is now set up for another 50 years of service. I'm very proud of what we've achieved," he says.

Chris McGuigan, commercial director of Trafalgar Entertainment which operates the theatre, said he was "tremendously excited" the Orchard's transformation was nearing completion.

"It's fantastic that the building will once again be welcoming audiences through its doors," he said.

McGuigan said he could see substantial progress every time he visited the site.

"It's a theatre with a unique connection to its community and we're determined to keep bringing great shows to the Orchard," he says.

Abbie Budden, who is making her debut as Cinderella at this year's panto, said the show would look "magical with the fantastic digital set".

"It would be special to be among the first performers in the refurbished theatre and to welcome audiences back for the first time," she added.

She said it was especially important to "bring the venue back to life" at a time when some theatres had shut in the country .

articles.title: Samoa PM apologises after Nazi salute video emerges
articles.summary: Pacific island nation’s leader says 2007 video showing him saying ‘Heil Hitler’ does not reflect his beliefs.
articles.body:
Samoa’s Prime Minister La’auli Leuatea Schmidt has apologised after previously unseen video showed him leading a Nazi salute and saying “Heil Hitler” at a family gathering.

Schmidt issued the apology on Monday after the Samoa Observer, a local newspaper, published the seven-second clip the previous day.

The footage was recorded at a Schmidt family reunion on the island of Savai‘i in July 2007, when he was an MP and deputy speaker of parliament.

In the video, Schmidt is holding a microphone as he leads a “hip hip” exchange with the group before telling those present to raise their right hands and say “Heil Hitler”.

About a dozen people visible in the footage appear to follow him.

Radio New Zealand said it had independently verified the footage through its correspondent in Samoa.

Schmidt said on Monday that the words and gesture were inappropriate regardless of what was intended at the gathering and apologised for the offence they could cause.

“I reject Nazism, antisemitism, racism and all forms of political extremism,” he said, adding that the episode did not represent his beliefs or the values of Samoa’s government and people.

The apology followed criticism from academics contacted by the Samoa Observer.

Richard Evans, a historian of Nazi Germany, told the Samoa Observer by email that the footage was “shocking and disturbing”.

The paper also quoted University of Canterbury academic Anne-Marie Brady as saying Schmidt should explain and apologise.

Schmidt, who became prime minister in 2025, has made strong public expressions of support for Israel.

He wore a Jewish prayer shawl at his swearing-in, where a shofar, a horn used in Jewish religious ceremonies, was sounded.

He has also pledged to open a Samoan embassy in Jerusalem before the end of 2026, a step taken by only a handful of countries because of the city’s disputed status and Palestinian claims to East Jerusalem as the capital of a future state.

In his Monday statement, Schmidt said he considered the controversy addressed and would focus on the country’s economic and social challenges.

articles.title: Tourism businesses encouraged to collaborate in Ironbridge Gorge
articles.summary: The National Trust is setting out its plans for the area and inviting businesses to get involved.
articles.body:
Tourism businesses in Shropshire have been invited to learn more about the National Trust's plans for the Ironbridge Gorge museums, and to how they can benefit.

The National Trust took over ownership of the sites in March and the attractions reopened under their new management in May.

The Telford and Shropshire Local Visitor Economy Partnership has arranged a one-day conference in Coalbrookdale on Monday to discuss collaboration opportunities.

It said the museums, which tell the story of the birth of the industrial revolution in the gorge, were one of the county's "most important visitor attractions".

The attractions had previously been managed by The Ironbridge Gorge Museum Trust since 1967.

It ran 10 museums, 35 listed buildings and scheduled monuments, including Blists Hill Victorian Town, the Coalbrookdale Museum of Iron and the Old Furnace.

It does not include the world's first large Iron Bridge, a Grade I listed structure spanning the River Severn and giving the area its name, which is owned by Telford and Wrekin Council and cared for by English Heritage.

When the National Trust took over, with the help of a £9m government grant, the National Trust said it aimed to increase annual visitor numbers from 330,000 to 600,000 in the long term.

That will partly be achieved by giving paid National Trust members access to the site, but it said it also wanted to "strengthen relationships" with the tourism industry in the area.

The Local Visitor Economy Partnership is made up of Telford and Wrekin Council, Shropshire Council, Visit Telford and Visit Shropshire.

It said the conference on Monday would allow businesses to "learn more about the evolving visitor offer at Ironbridge Gorge, gain insight into future opportunities, and explore how businesses can work alongside one of the destination's strongest visitor assets".

The Ironbridge Gorge area was named a Unesco World heritage site in 1986.

It played a key role in the Industrial Revolution, owing much to Abraham Darby I's transformation of iron production, as well as the "iron masters" who followed him, with some likening the area to the silicon valley of its day.

The innovations which were started there are widely recognised as being the catalyst for the building of the bridges, railways and machinery of the modern world.

The £9m government grant, announced last October , was given to enable the National Trust to fund the upkeep of the properties, as part of the government's Plan for Change, to help boost the local economy.

articles.title: Lampard Inquiry considers early findings on Essex deaths
articles.summary: Early recommendations could be issued if evidence highlights patient safety risks, the chair says.
articles.body:
The chair of a public inquiry into mental health deaths said she would make interim recommendations if she identified issues that "might pose an urgent risk to patient safety".

Baroness Kate Lampard is examining the deaths of more than 2,000 people who died while under the care of Essex mental health services between 2000 and the end of 2023.

The Lampard Inquiry will hear further evidence during hearings beginning on 5 October before deciding whether recommendations were needed ahead of a final report, Baroness Lampard said.

Any recommendations were expected to focus on inpatient safety, including resuscitation procedures and monitoring technology used to detect patients in distress.

"Those two matters are not specific to Essex and therefore the evidence the inquiry hears will be of relevance to service providers across the entire country," Baroness Lampard said.

"It may carry implications for the care and treatment provided on all mental health units."

One system under examination as part of the inquiry is Oxevision, which can take footage, record breathing and pulse rates and is used by a number of NHS mental health trusts in England.

Concerns have been raised about privacy, dignity and whether the technology could be used as a substitute for face-to-face care.

Tammy Smith, whose daughter Sophie Alderman died in 2022, previously told the inquiry: "It actually takes away human interaction. They are at their most vulnerable.

"They need those conversations. They need someone to ask, 'Are you OK? Do you need anything?' We all need that."

What is the Lampard Inquiry and what could it change?

Lampard Inquiry: Five things we've learned so far

The company behind Oxevision, LIO Health, said the technology helped prevent serious incidents, supports staff in providing care and reduces time spent on paperwork.

NHS England said any vision-based monitoring technology must support a human rights-based approach to care and be used in line with legal requirements and appropriate patient consent.

The inquiry is due to hear evidence from NHS England, the Care Quality Commission and the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency during hearings between 5 and 15 October.

The latest sessions will take place at Chelmsford Civic Centre rather than in London, where previous hearings have been held.

Families will then be invited to give their views on possible recommendations during a virtual hearing on 20 October, before Baroness Lampard decides whether interim recommendations should be issued.

The inquiry's final report, which could have national implications for mental health services across England, is not expected until 2028.

articles.title: Middle East oil exports surpass pre-war levels despite tensions, data shows
articles.summary: IRGC commander says oil flows through US-supervised route in Hormuz are ‘negligible’.
articles.body:
Crude oil exports from the Middle East have risen above pre-war levels on four of the seven days in the last week of September, provisional data from ship-tracking firm Kpler showed.

However, senior Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) commander Ali Fadavi said in a televised interview on Sunday night that only three to four million barrels of oil per day (bpd) are now moving through the route, dismissing the amount as “negligible” when compared with pre-war traffic.

Fadavi said, for the first time, no US vessels were present in the Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz, the Sea of Oman or even the northern Indian Ocean and US warships are “100 percent vulnerable” to IRGC attacks.

Kpler data showed crude exports from the region exceeded pre-war levels on September 24 and between September 27 and 29, rising to 19.5-22.5 million bpd.

Around that time, Iran claimed success in attacking ships – including US Navy vessels – near the Strait of Hormuz, saying the strikes had forced Washington to move its warships further from the Iranian coast.

Before the US-Israel war on Iran began, exports averaged 18 million bpd between March 2025 and February 2026.

According to Kpler data, the overall tally for crude, oil products, chemicals and non-gas liquids averaged 22.4 million bpd in the seven days to September 30.

On October 1, the seven-day moving average for crude exports was at 18.5 million bpd. This includes transits via the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, exports from terminals and ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman.

The number of liquefied natural gas cargoes exiting the Strait of Hormuz also rose in September to its highest monthly level since February.

The figures exclude any vessels that might have crossed the strait with their automatic identification system transponders turned off to avoid detection.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency reported at least one attack a day in the Strait of Hormuz or in the Gulf of Aden since October 2.

On Sunday, Iran’s top negotiator and parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until the United States accepts Tehran’s seven-day plan to reopen the waterway.

The U.S. Southern Command said the vessel was traveling along "established narco-trafficking routes" in the Caribbean. The military shared a video that showed what appeared to be an explosion destroying a moving boat it described as a go-fast vessel. "Under the direction of U.S. Southern Command, Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere executed a lethal, kinetic strike on a go-fast vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Caribbean," the military said in a statement. US FORCES OBLITERATE SUSPECTED 'NARCO-TERRORIST' VESSEL IN LETHAL EASTERN PACIFIC STRIKE, KILLING 3 Southern Command claimed that intelligence revealed the vessel's "active involvement in narco-trafficking." The military did not provide evidence to back up this allegation. "The operation killed four narco-terrorists," the statement added. This is the latest attack that the Trump administration has argued was launched in an attempt to eliminate alleged narco-terrorists, with the death toll in these strikes carried out since September 2025 sitting at more than 235. The Pentagon has refused to release the identities of those killed in the strikes since last year. It has also refused to provide evidence of drugs on board. The administration has been scrutinized in the past year by Democrats and even some Republicans, including Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., who has raised concerns about killing people without due process and the possibility of killing innocent people. The attacks have also been denounced by human rights groups as "extrajudicial killings." Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth said during a visit to Panama in August that Colombia, Guatemala and Honduras had agreed to allow the U.S. to carry out joint military operations against criminal groups on their soil, although Guatemala denied reaching a deal. articles.title: Hemel Hempstead tea shop may close despite Ludwig filming
articles.summary: The series, starring David Mitchell, is filming scenes in Hemel Hempstead.
articles.body:
A tea room being used to film the third series of Ludwig starring David Mitchell could close permanently unless it raises £25,000.

Trustees of the volunteer-run Liberty Tea Rooms and Community Hub in Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire, said the charity was in an "extremely low cash position".

Mark Kitson, chairman of the trustees, said the series being filmed at the venue had created a real buzz and it had been good to hire it out "at a time that we really need the extra funds".

The tea room is temporarily closed until 7 October while filming takes place for Ludwig; its frontage has been transformed to resemble a bank, which it was before becoming a community venue.

The charity has already reduced staffing costs, but trustees said it would close permanently unless it raised £25,000 by the end of October.

Kitson said: "Lots of towns and high streets are having tough times at the moment.

"When you come into the Tea Rooms, someone will welcome you, talk to you if you want a chat, offer a meal if you need it, and can also provide debt advice or a food bank parcel.

"You might just want tea and a scone, but if you need something more, we will do our very best to help you."

Filming will take place inside and outside the building over several weeks, with a rain machine due to be used for one scene.

Kitson said the production team would restore the tea room once filming was completed, as well as repairing a broken window and updating its signage.

He added: "The filming has been brilliant. It's created a real buzz and excitement on Hemel Hempstead High Street, and for our team and volunteers, they have also paid us a fee for being in the building at a time that we really need the extra funds."
